
```{r column info}
# what columns do we have?
colnames(Life_Expectancy_Data)
# there are 22 different columns
str(Life_Expectancy_Data)
#  columns contain character data, 8 contain integer data,
# and 12 contain numeric data.
summary(Life_Expectancy_Data)

```

```{r row info} 
# how many countries
length(unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country))
length(unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country[Life_Expectancy_Data$Status == "Developing"]))
length(unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country[Life_Expectancy_Data$Status == "Developed"]))
# what years included?
range(Life_Expectancy_Data$Year)

```

```{r}
table(Life_Expectancy_Data$Year)
#2013 has more occurences, how?
#investigate below
```
```{r}
#which countries are in 2013 that are not in 2012?
uc_2013 = unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country[Life_Expectancy_Data$Year == 2013])
uc_2012 = unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country[Life_Expectancy_Data$Year == 2012])
print("Countries in 2013 not in 2012:")
setdiff(uc_2013, uc_2012)
```

``` {r scores and rankings}
# top 5 highest and lowest countries per category(life expectancy, GDP, ) per year (2000 & 2015?). standardise by population? -> make new df with standardised per category of interest. or is it already standardised? check WHO
#maybe take the top 5 from 2000, follow them over the years?
#applied piping like we learned. any other new techniques?

class(Life_Expectancy_Data)
  
Life_Expectancy_Data %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  slice_max(Life_expectancy, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

Life_Expectancy_Data %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  slice_min(Life_expectancy, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

```
